o: On a circular array we may cut it into at most k contiguous arcs (possibly wrapping) and score each arc as max - min, maximizing the total. For [1,2,3,3] with k=2 the wrapped split [2,3],[3,1] scores 1+2=3; with k=1 the whole circle scores 2; larger k cannot beat 3 here. Since n, k <= 1000, an O(k * n^2) range DP is the intended scale. Key structural fact: the arc containing the global maximum can be assumed to wrap, so rotating the array so the maximum sits at index 0 lets us solve a purely linear partition problem.
k: Rotating so the maximum element is first makes the optimal cyclic partition equivalent to a linear one (cut at the maximum).
Splitting an arc never decreases total range, so 'at most k' parts means the DP over exactly j parts, maximized over j <= k, is correct.
dp[j][i] = best score for the first i elements in exactly j arcs, extended by maintaining running max/min while moving the previous cut point p.

a.i: Rotate the array to start at its maximum, then run the standard partition DP where each transition extends the last arc leftward while maintaining its running max and min in O(1), giving the arc's range for free.
s: Rotate nums so the maximum element is at index 0.
dp[0][0] = 0; for j = 1..k and i = j..n, sweep p from i-1 down to j-1 updating running max/min of a[p..i-1] and dp[j][i] = max(dp[j-1][p] + max - min).
Answer = max over j in [1, k] of dp[j][n].
Optionally stop early when a whole dp layer stops improving.
a.t: O(k * n^2) - for each of k layers, each endpoint i sweeps all cut positions p with O(1) range maintenance
a.sp: O(k * n) for the DP table (rolling rows reduce it to O(n))

w: Explain the rotation-at-maximum reduction carefully - it is the crux that turns a cyclic problem linear. Pitfalls: scoring exactly k parts when fewer may be better (take max over j), letting arcs be empty, and 32-bit overflow of range sums in Java/C++. Follow-up: minimize the total range, or require exactly k parts.
